name: The Ouroboros Interval

detectability.signature: An identical distress beacon burst repeating every six hours, word for word, down to the static

proximity: Instruments begin reporting readings from six hours in the future
Crew experience fleeting déjà vu aligned to the coming reset
contact: Actions and conversations repeat verbatim regardless of intent
Vessels find themselves returned to their entry coordinates at each chime
prolonged_exposure: Captives relive the same six hours indefinitely, memories resetting with the cycle
Psychological collapse from uncounted identical repetitions

phenomena: Visible echoes of the same events replaying across the volume
Causality loops bleeding into neighboring systems' sensor logs
Objects existing in multiple timeframes simultaneously at each reset
hazards: Trapped in time loop with memory reset each cycle
Memory loss and temporal disorientation upon escape
opportunities: Recovery of lost ships and personnel caught mid-loop
Unique research opportunity into closed causal curves
known_incidents: The survey vessel Perpetua logged four hundred identical days before rescuers matched her beacon's repetition to the cycle
One crewman of the Perpetua retains fragmentary memories across loops and is now studied more closely than the anomaly itself
description: Within a sphere fifty-two thousand kilometers wide, the same six hours occur, and occur, and occur. Observers outside see the volume shimmer faintly at each reset, like heat lightning, while the distress call of a ship twenty years dead repeats inside with perfect fidelity. The loop is exact: every bolt of static falls in the same place.

Entry costs nothing; the boundary does not resist. Inside, events march identically regardless of interference, and at each chime of the cycle, matter, minds, and momentum return to their starting states. Objects straddling the edge exist twice for the length of a heartbeat before the universe tidies them back into one.

The survey ship Perpetua revealed the Interval's nature when her looping distress burst was finally matched to the six-hour chime. Her logs contain four hundred identical days, each crewman writing the same entries in slowly diverging handwriting. How the loop began, and whether the wreck inside is cause or captive, remains unanswered.

Salvage teams work the boundary in shifts timed to the reset, recovering material that will simply be restored six hours later, a fact that torments accountants. One Perpetua survivor remembers across iterations, imperfectly, and lives under quiet institutional observation. Negotiations with the loop itself have been formally proposed; no one claims to know how.
